newsitem.title: USA: Bumper crop of initiatives on U.S. ballots.
newsitem.headline: Bumper crop of initiatives on U.S. ballots.

text.p: Proposals to legalise marijuana use by the sick in California, stop aerial hunting of wolves in Alaska and ban razing Maine forests are among a host of statewide initiatives before U.S. voters next week.

Colorado voters will decide on a controversial parental rights initiative, Californians may end many state affirmative action programmes and Florida residents will vote on a proposal to tax sugar and use the proceeds to restore the Everglades.
Voters in 20 states will be scratching their heads Tuesday over 89 initiatives, the most since 1914, according to the Public Affairs Research Institute of New Jersey.

Citizens are empowered to change the law through the initiative process in 24 states. If they can gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, supporters can go directly to voters on often controversial issues, avoiding state legislatures.

But the high cost makes it difficult for ordinary citizens to get a proposal on the ballot and the initiative process is increasingly used by interest groups, Joan Ponessa, research director with the non-partisan research institute, says.
More than $200 million is expected to be spent this year by supporters and opponents of the various measures.

A group called U.S. Term Limits is coordinating an initiative campaign in 14 states pushing legislators to support limits on how long members of Congress can remain in office. Under the proposal, lawmakers who oppose a constitutional amendment on congressional term limits would be identified on the ballot when they seek re-election.

California, often a trend-setter, has several of the most controversial initiatives this year. One being closely watched around the nation would bar many state affirmative action programmes of the kind used since the 1960s to increase opportunities for racial minorities and women.

Another California initiative would make it legal for the sick to smoke marijuana when advised by a doctor. Supporters say marijuana can help ease the pain of AIDS, cancer and glaucoma sufferers, but opponents see this measure, and a similar proposal on the ballot in Arizona, as attempts to legalise marijuana through the back door.

The business community is watching a California initiative that would make it easier to sue for securities fraud. Backers say it punishes white collar cheaters who defraud people out of their pension savings. Opponents, many in high-tech Silicon Valley, say it could make California courts a magnet for class action lawsuits and send stock prices reeling. They are spending more than $30 million to fight the measure.

Several states have initiatives that would bar some hunting methods. Activists in Alaska are seeking to ban hunters from tracking wolves and other predators by airplane and then landing and shooting them the same day.
In Michigan, sportsmen, motel owners and others are up in arms about a proposal that would outlaw the use of hounds and bait to hunt bear, the most common way the sport is done.

Florida voters are being asked to approve a constitutional amendment to charge farmers a penny-a-pound tax on raw sugar grown in the Everglades. The measure is the result of a long-running battle between cane farmers and environmentalists over polluted water that leeches from farms into the famous "river of grass" that is home to alligators, deer, endangered Florida panthers and many species of bird and insect.

The campaign has proved the costliest in Florida's history and one of the most expensive in the nation, with nearly $27 million spent by the two sides. Sugar farmers say the tax, designed to raise $900 million for Everglades restoration over its 25-year life, would sound a death knell for the industry.

A controversial Colorado initiative would amend the state constitution to recognise the right of parents to "direct and control the upbringing, education, values and discipline of their children." Supporters say it would strengthen the family but opponents maintain it would give parents a free hand to abuse their children without fear of legal retribution.
